readings.c1s1:
¶
'''twistle<sup>2</sup>''' (twis′l), ''n.'' Same as ''twissel.'' ''Halliwell.''

'''twist-machine''' (twist′ma-shēn″), ''n.'' A form of lace-making machine. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''twist-stitch''' (twist′stich), ''n.'' Same as ''cord-stitch.'' ''Dict. of Needlework.''

'''twist-tobacco''' (twist′tō-bak″ō), ''n.'' See ''tobacco.''

'''twist-velocity''' (twist′vē-los″i-ti), ''n.'' The state of a body at any instant when it has a rotational velocity round a certain axis compounded with a linear velocity along that axis.

'''twisty''' (twis′ti), ''n.'' [< ''twist'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] See ''Helicteres.''

'''twit''' (twit), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''twitted'', ppr. ''twitting.'' [Formerly also ''twite, twight;'' by apheresis from ''atwite,'' < ME. ''atwiten,'' < AS. ''ætwitan,'' reproach, < ''æt-'' (see ''at-''<sup>1</sup>) + ''witan,'' reproach: see ''wite.''] '''1.''' To reproach; upbraid, especially with past follies, errors, or offenses; annoy by reproaches; taunt.
{{smaller block|I ''twhyte'' one, I caste hym in the tethe or in the nose. Je luy reprouche. . . . This terme is also northren.
{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 764.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And evermore she did him sharpely ''twight''
For breach of faith to her, which he had firmely plight.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. vi. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|Alas! what should I touch their parents, or ''twit'' them by their other friends? ''G. Harvey'', Four Letters.}}
'''2.''' To charge or reproach with; upbraid on account of; bring forward as a taunt.
{{smaller block|Envy, why ''twit’st'' thou me my time’s spent ill?
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Shall they [Papists] ''twit'' us that Our Father hath taken from the church what their Paternoster bestowed on it?}}
readings.c2s2:
{{smaller block|Strong yoke for a hog, with a ''twicher'' and rings.
{{right|''Tusser'', September’s Husbandry, Husbandly Furniture, [st. 17.}}}}

'''twitch-grass''' (twich′grȧs), ''n.'' Quitch-grass; twitch.

'''twitching''' (twich′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] The act of one who or that which twitches; especially, an involuntary convulsive jerking of the muscles, etc. See ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 2.

{{smaller block|On the coarser semi-convulsive movements, ''twitchings'', jerkings, and grimacings not rarely met with in hysteria I do not dwell.
{{right|''Lancet'', 1890, I. 284.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Fibrillary twitching''', irregular spasmodic contraction of the fibrils of a muscle independent of each other.}}

'''twite<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' An obsolete form of ''twit.''

'''twite<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v.'' A variant of ''thwite.''

{{smaller block|<poem>They ne rekke in what wyse, where ne when,
Nor how vngoodly they on theyre mete ''twyte.''</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 7.}}}}

'''twite<sup>3</sup>''' (twīt), ''n.'' [Said to be imitative of the cry of the bird.] A kind of linnet, the mountain-linnet, ''Linaria montium'' or ''L. flavirostris'', a European bird of the family ''Fringillidæ'', nearly related to the redpoll, siskin, and goldfinch.

'''twite-finch''' (twīt′finch), ''n.'' The twite.

'''twit-lark''' (twit′lärk), ''n.'' A titlark or pipit. [Prov. Eng.]

'''twitter<sup>1</sup>''' (twit′ėr), ''v.'' [< ME. ''twiteren'', ''twitren'' = D. ''kwetteren'' = OHG. ''zwizirōn'', MHG. ''zwitzern'', G. ''zwitschern'' = Sw. ''quittra'' = Dan. ''kvidre'', twitter; prob. orig. imitative.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To utter a succession of small, tremulous sounds, as a bird; sing in bird-notes; chirp.
readings.c2s3:
<poem>{{smaller|The breezy call of incense-breathing Morn,
The swallow ''twitt’ring'' from the straw-built shed.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Gray'', Elegy.}}}}
'''2.''' To titter; giggle. [Obsolete or provincial.]
{{smaller block|How the fool bridles! How she ''twitters'' at him!
{{right|''Fletcher'', Pilgrim, iii. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' To quiver; tremble; palpitate; hence, to be in a flutter or fright. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|My Heart ''Twitters.'' ''Ray'', Eng. Words (1691), p. 77.}}
{{smaller block|How the slave ''twitters!'' You look not up at greatness; you mind too much the worldly things that are beneath you. ''Brome'', Sparagus Garden, iii. 5.}}
{{smaller block|To the unhinged toper and the ''twittering'' child, a huge bulk of blackness seemed to sweep down.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Scribner’s Mag., IV. 511.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To sing or utter in bird-notes; chirp out.
<poem>{{smaller|Some small bird, half awake,
''Twittered'' an early ditty for his sake.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''R. H. Stoddard'', The King’s Bell.}}}}
'''2.''' To spin unevenly. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|To ''twitter'' thread or yarn. ''Ray'', Eng. Words (1691), p. 77.}}

'''twitter<sup>1</sup>''' (twit′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''twitter''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' A chirp or series of chirps, as of a bird, especially the swallow.
<poem>{{smaller|Hark, ’tis the sparrows’ good-night ''twitter''
About your cottage eaves!}}</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Browning'', The Lost Mistress.}}}}
'''2.''' A fit of laughter; a titter. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''3.''' A tremble; a flutter; a general excitement; a pother: as, to be in (or of) a ''twit-''

''ter'', or to be in or on the ''twitters''. [Prov. Eng. and U. S.]
{{smaller block|I am all of a ''twitter'' to see my old John Harrowby again.
{{right|''Colman and Garrick'', Clandestine Marriage, i. 1.}}
<poem>This hangin’ on mont’ arter mont’
Fer one sharp purpose ’mongst the ''twitter'',
I tell you, it doos kind o’ stunt
The peth and sperit of a critter.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Biglow Papers, 2d ser., vii.}}}}

¶'''twitter<sup>2</sup>''' (twit′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''twit'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who twits or reproaches. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''twitter<sup>3</sup>''' (twit′ėr), ''n.'' [Perhaps a dial. corruption of ''flitter''<sup>1</sup> or ''fritter''.] A shred; a fragment: used in the plural. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twitter<sup>4</sup>''' (twit′ėr), ''n.'' [A dial. var. of ''quitter''<sup>2</sup>.] The refuse or residuum of the case of the sperm-whale, a gummy and thready substance left when the case is squeezed.

'''twitteration''' (twit-ė-rā′shon), ''n.'' [< ''twitter''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ation''.] A twitter; a flutter. [Slang.]
{{smaller block|When they struck up our blood-stirrin’ national air, it made me feel all over in a ''twitteration'', as if I was on wires a’most, considerable martial.
{{right|''Haliburton'', The Clockmaker, p. 373. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''twitter-bit''' (twit′ėr-bit), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] The bottom of the countersink receiving the head of the screw which holds the blades of scissors together. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''twitter-bone''' (twit′ėr-bōn), ''n.'' [< ''twitter''<sup>4</sup>, as a var. of ''quitter''<sup>2</sup>, + ''bone''<sup>1</sup>.] An excrescence on a horse’s hoof, due to a contraction. ''Halliwell.''

{{smaller block|All that ever he did was not worth so much as the ''twittle-twattle'' that he maketh.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 85.}}}}

'''twit-twat''' (twit′twot), ''n.'' [Imitative.] The European house-sparrow, ''Passer domesticus.'' See cut under ''Passer.''

'''’twixt''' (twikst), ''prep.'' An abbreviation of ''betwixt.''
{{smaller block|<poem>It shall be cause of war and dire events,
And set dissension ''’twixt'' the son and sire.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1160.}}}}

'''’twixt-brain''' (twikst′brān), ''n.'' Same as ''’tweenbrain. Gegenbaur'', Comp. Anat. (trans.), p. 503.

'''twizzle''' (twiz′l), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''twizzled'', ppr. ''twizzling.'' [A var. of *''twissel'', ''v.'', lit. ‘double,’ < ''twissel'', ''a.''] To roll and twist. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|If a couple of waxed-ends [in the game of “cob-nut”] became ''twizzled'', the boy who first could shout—
<poem>Twizzler, twizzler!
My fost blow—</poem>
took the first stroke when the waxed-ends were untwisted.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., IX. 138.}}}}

{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 764.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And evermore she did him sharpely ''twight''
For breach of faith to her, which he had firmely plight.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. vi. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|Alas! what should I touch their parents, or ''twit'' them by their other friends? ''G. Harvey'', Four Letters.}}
'''2.''' To charge or reproach with; upbraid on account of; bring forward as a taunt.
{{smaller block|Envy, why ''twit’st'' thou me my time’s spent ill?
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Shall they [Papists] ''twit'' us that Our Father hath taken from the church what their Paternoster bestowed on it? {{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 469.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To twit in the teeth†''', to taunt maliciously; cast offensive facts or charges in the teeth of. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, v. ='''Syn.''' ''Chaff'', ''Mock'', etc. See ''taunt''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''twit''' (twit), ''n.'' [< ''twit'', ''v.''] A reproach; a taunt; an upbraiding or gibing reminder or insinuation.
{{smaller block|Upon Condition there be no ''Twits'' of the Good Man departed. ''Etherege'', Love in a Tub, v. 5.}}

'''twitch'''<sup>1</sup> (twich), ''v.'' [< ME. ''twicchen'', ''twichen'', also ''twikkin'' (pret. ''twight'', ''twyght'', ''twighte'', ''twiȝte''), < AS. ''twiccian'', twitch, pull, = LG. ''twikken'' = OHG. *''zwicchēn'', MHG. G. ''zwicken'', fasten with nails, shut in, peg, pin, grip, nip, twitch; cf. G. ''zwick'', a nip, pinch. Cf. ''twick'', ''tweak''<sup>1</sup>, ''twig''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To pull or draw with a hasty jerk; snatch; jerk away.
{{smaller block|<poem>His swerde anon out of his shethe he ''twyghte.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1185.}}
My cap ’s quite gone: where the villain ''twitched'' it, I don’t know. {{right|''Miss Burney'', Evelina, xxxiv.}}
<poem>Saint Praxed in a glory, and one Pan
Ready to ''twitch'' the nymph’s last garment off.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', The Bishop Orders his Tomb.}}}}
'''2.''' To give a short, sudden pull or tug at; jerk at; cause to move quickly or spasmodically.
{{smaller block|Petit-André, slapping the other shoulder, called out, “Courage, my fair son! since you must begin the dance, let the ball open gaily, for all the rebecs are in tune,” ''twitching'' the halter at the same time, to give point to his joke. {{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, vi.}}}}
'''3.''' To nip; squeeze; make fast; tie tightly. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Be the neck sche hym ''twyghte'',
And let hym hange all nyghte.</poem>
{{right|''MS. Cantab.'', Ff. ii. 38, f. 117. (''Halliwell.'')}} <poem>''Sub.'' And shall we ''twitch'' him?
''Face.'' Thorough both the gills.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|They ''twitch'' the offender about the waste with a towell . . . untill they have drawn him within the compasse of a span.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 49.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be suddenly jerked; move or contract quickly or spasmodically, as a muscle.
{{smaller block|They [movements] vary, in sensitive frogs and with a proper amount of irritation, so little as almost to resemble in their machine-like regularity the performances of a jumping-jack, whose legs must ''twitch'' whenever you pull the string.
{{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychol., I. 15.}}}}
'''2.''' To carp; sneer; make flings. Compare ''jerk''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. i.'', 2.
{{smaller block|Try to barter one with the other amicably, and not to ''twitch'' and carp.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Diogenes and Plato.}}}}

'''twitch'''<sup>1</sup> (twich), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''twich''; < ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' Cf. ''twick'', ''twig''<sup>2</sup>, ''tweak''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A short, sharp pull or tug; a jerk or snatch.
{{smaller block|I felt him take hold of my flesh, and give me such a deadly ''twitch'' back that I thought he had pulled part of me after himself.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}
'''2.''' A short, spastic contraction of the fibers of muscles; a stitch; a twinge: as, a ''twitch'' in the side; convulsive ''twitches''; especially, such a movement when causing pain: sometimes applied to moral pangs.
{{smaller block|<poem>So crackt their backe bones wrincht
With horrid ''twitches''.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xxiii. 620.}}}}

{{smaller block|These ''twitches'' of Conscience argue there are some quick touches left of the sence of good and evil.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. ii.}}}}
'''3†.''' A pair of nippers or tweezers.
{{smaller block|Take therefore a ''twich'' of silver, and therewith lift up subtilly the ungle from the tunicle, proceeding to the lachrimall where it grew, and there cut it away.
{{right|''Barrough’s Method of Physick'' (1624). (''Nares.'')}}}}
'''4.''' A noose attached to a stock or handle and twisted around the upper lip of a horse so as to bring him under command when shoeing or clipping: an instrument used for holding a vicious horse.—'''5.''' In ''mining'', a sudden narrowing of a vein so that the walls come nearly or quite together. [North. Eng.]

'''twitch'''<sup>2</sup> (twich), ''v.'' A dialectal variant of ''touch.'' ''Halliwell.''

'''twitch'''<sup>3</sup> (twich), ''n.'' [A dial. var. of ''quitch''<sup>2</sup>.] The quitch or quitch-grass, ''Agropyrum repens.'' {{smaller|The name is also applied to the bent-grass, ''Agrostis vulgaris'', and to a few other grasses, as the sheep’s-fescue, ''Festuca ovina'', called ''black twitch.''}}

'''twitchel'''<sup>1</sup> (twich′el), ''n.'' [< ''twitch''<sup>1</sup> + ''-el.''] A narrow passage; an alley. Compare ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 5. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|All persons passing by this ''Twitchel'' are requested to go up or down directly, without loitering, causing obstruction, etc. {{right|Quoted in ''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VII. 275.}}}}

'''twitchel'''<sup>2</sup> (twich′el), ''n.'' [A var. of ''twichild.''] A childish old man. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twitcher''' (twich′ėr), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''twicher''; < ''twitch''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who or that which twitches.—'''2.''' ''pl.'' Small pincers. ''Halliwell.''—'''3†.''' An instrument used for clinching hog-rings. ''Davies.'' {{smaller block|Strong yoke for a hog, with a ''twicher'' and rings.
{{right|''Tusser'', September’s Husbandry, Husbandly Furniture, [st. 17.}}}}

'''twitch-grass''' (twich′grȧs), ''n.'' Quitch-grass; twitch.

'''twittering''' (twit′ėr-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''twitter''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The chirping of birds; also, any series of small, clear, intermitted sounds resembling the notes of a bird.

'''2.''' A quivering; a flutter; a state of tremulous excitement indicative of alarm, suspense, desire, etc.

{{smaller block|A widow which had a ''twittering'' towards a second husband took a gossipping companion to manage the job.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}

'''twitterlight†''' (twit′ėr-līt), ''n.'' Twilight.

<poem>You can steal secretly hither . . .
At twilight, ''twitter-lights!''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Middleton'', Your Five Gallants, v. 1.}}}}

'''twittingly''' (twit′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a twitting manner; with taunts.

{{smaller block|In a long letter, having reckoned all his civilities to the English nation, he ''twittingly'' upbraided them there-with.
{{right|''Camden'', Hist. Queen Elizabeth, an. 1569. (''Richardson.'')}}}}

'''twittle†''' (twit′l), ''v. t.'' [A var. of ''tittle''<sup>1</sup>; cf. ''twitter''<sup>1</sup> in sense of ''titter''<sup>2</sup>.] To chatter; babble; tattle.

{{smaller block|His hystorie . . . ''twitled'' . . . tales out of schoole.
{{right|''Stanihurst'', Epistle to Sir H. Sidney (Æneid, ed. Arber, Int., [p. xi.).}}}}

'''twittle-twattle†''' (twit′l-twot″l), ''n.'' [< ''twittle'' + ''twattle'', or a varied redupl. of ''twattle''.] Tittle-tattle; gabble. {{smaller block|All that ever he did was not worth so much as the ''twittle-twattle'' that he maketh.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 85.}}}}

'''twit-twat''' (twit′twot), ''n.'' [Imitative.] The European house-sparrow, ''Passer domesticus.'' See cut under ''Passer.''

'''’twixt''' (twikst), ''prep.'' An abbreviation of ''betwixt.''
{{smaller block|<poem>It shall be cause of war and dire events,
And set dissension ''’twixt'' the son and sire.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1160.}}}}

'''’twixt-brain''' (twikst′brān), ''n.'' Same as ''’tweenbrain. Gegenbaur'', Comp. Anat. (trans.), p. 503.

'''twizzle''' (twiz′l), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''twizzled'', ppr. ''twizzling.'' [A var. of *''twissel'', ''v.'', lit. ‘double,’ < ''twissel'', ''a.''] To roll and twist. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|If a couple of waxed-ends [in the game of “cob-nut”] became ''twizzled'', the boy who first could shout—
<poem>Twizzler, twizzler!
My fost blow—</poem>
took the first stroke when the waxed-ends were untwisted.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., IX. 138.}}}}
